scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The document is a German nationwide cross-sectional survey of informal caregivers of people with dementia concerning medication-process-related caregiver burden; it never mentions Lyme disease or Long COVID, so it does not map to the lyme/long_covid/both categories and is marked unclear within that fixed enum, even though the document's own focus (dementia caregiving) is clear.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a German nationwide survey of 180 informal caregivers of people with dementia examining the burden caregivers feel from managing medications ('medication process' or MP-related burden), alongside the validated Zarit Burden Interview for general caregiver burden. It finds that patient-facing tasks (explaining medication information, accompanying to appointments, reminding about doses) were rated as more burdensome than logistical tasks (collecting prescriptions, preparing doses). Support from community nurses did not measurably reduce either general or MP-related burden, and caregivers valued fast service and thorough counselling from community pharmacies more than organisational services like delivery or app-based ordering. The study reports no dollar costs, time-use, or income-loss figures; its findings are limited to self-reported burden percentages and a validated burden-interview score from a convenience sample recruited through dementia caregiver self-help groups.

Time pressure experienced by caregivers when visiting community pharmacies is discussed qualitatively but not measured in hours or frequency.

evidence_gaps: No direct medical costs, out-of-pocket spending, or pharmacy/medication expenditures were collected for either patients or caregivers.
No data on caregiving hours, lost income, employment impact, or productivity loss were collected.
No data on insurance, access barriers, or diagnostic delay for the underlying dementia diagnosis were collected.
The design is cross-sectional with no follow-up, so long-term financial or health consequences of MP-related burden cannot be assessed.
No stratification of burden outcomes by dementia severity/stage, caregiver sex, age, or relationship type was reported.
comparison_boundaries: No price/cost figures of any kind are reported in this document, so there is nothing here that could be pooled with cost data from other sources or price years.
The sample was recruited exclusively through dementia caregiver self-help groups in Germany; findings should not be generalized to caregivers outside support networks or to other countries.

The 8-item MP-related burden scale is a newly developed, non-validated instrument distinct from the validated short-form Zarit Burden Interview; their scores were tested for correlation (not significant) but should not be treated as interchangeable or combined into a single burden metric.

Percentages reporting '(very) high burden' per MP task are single cross-sectional snapshot figures for this German sample only and should not be combined with burden percentages from differently defined scales or other populations.

decision_relevance.summary: This document's findings could inform dementia care delivery teams, community pharmacies, and nursing services in Germany (and similar health systems) about which specific medication-process tasks drive caregiver burden, and about where current community-nurse support does and does not help. It does not support any cost or payer-facing simulation, since no dollar amounts, time-use, or income-loss figures are reported. Patient/caregiver advocates could use the item-level burden breakdown to argue for communication-focused pharmacy and clinical interventions rather than purely logistical support services.
use_cases: A community pharmacy or dementia caregiver support organization could use the item-level burden percentages (27.3% for communicating medication information vs. 4.4% for obtaining medications) to prioritize counselling-based services over logistics-only services like delivery.

spec.title: Dementia Caregiver Medication-Process Burden (German Survey, n=180)
spec.boundary: This simulation reflects a German nationwide cross-sectional survey of 180 informal caregivers of people with dementia, examining self-reported burden from medication-related tasks ('medication process' burden) and a validated general caregiver burden score (Zarit Burden Interview, short form). It covers only self-reported percentages and scale scores from this single survey wave; it does not include any dollar costs, caregiving hours, income loss, or federal/national data, and findings should not be generalized beyond caregivers recruited through German dementia self-help groups.

takeaway.patient: In this survey of 180 family caregivers of people with dementia in Germany, caregivers rated tasks that involve talking with the patient about medicines, going along to doctor visits, and reminding about doses as more tiring than simply picking up prescriptions or organizing pill doses. Caregivers who already had help from a community nurse did not report meaningfully less burden overall or with medication tasks specifically than those without that help, so nurse support alone may not address these communication-heavy parts of care. Caregivers also said fast service and thorough counseling from the pharmacy mattered more to them than delivery or app-based ordering.
takeaway.care: Among surveyed informal caregivers (n=180), interpersonal and decision-related medication tasks - explaining medication information, accompanying to appointments, and reminding about doses - were rated as burdensome by a much larger share of caregivers (18-27%) than purely logistical tasks such as collecting prescriptions or preparing doses (4-6%). Current community-nurse support, received by about 38% of caregivers, was not associated with a statistically significant reduction in either general caregiver burden or medication-process burden, suggesting existing nursing support may be addressing physical/logistical care needs without touching the communication and decision-support components driving burden. Caregivers also prioritized fast service and in-depth counseling from community pharmacies well above organisational conveniences like apps or delivery.
takeaway.policy: This survey-based evidence indicates that within this German sample, medication-related caregiver burden is concentrated in communication and decision-support tasks rather than logistics, and that current community-nurse support coverage (about 38% of caregivers) is not statistically associated with lower general or medication-process burden scores. No cost, utilization, or productivity data were collected, so this cannot support cost-effectiveness or budget-impact conclusions; it instead points to a gap in how existing community-based support services are structured relative to where caregivers report the most strain.

patient: If you support someone with dementia's medications, consider raising with your care team which specific tasks feel hardest for you - explaining medicine information, going to appointments, or reminders - rather than assuming all medication help needs are the same.

If a community nurse is already involved, this survey's finding suggests their support may not by itself reduce the communication-heavy parts of medication management; it may be worth asking what additional support exists for those specific tasks.

When choosing or evaluating a pharmacy, you may want to ask about wait times and the depth of medication counseling offered, since caregivers in this survey valued those over delivery or app-based ordering.
Keep in mind this reflects one German survey of caregivers connected to self-help groups; your own experience and what is available to you may differ.
care: This finding on which medication-process tasks caregivers rate as most burdensome (communication and appointment-related tasks vs. logistics) may be worth checking against your own program's service mix before assuming logistical support (delivery, prescription pickup) is what caregivers need most.

Given that community-nurse involvement was not associated with lower burden on these specific tasks in this sample, consider whether nurse training or care-coordination protocols could be extended to cover communication and decision-support roles, rather than only physical/logistical caregiving tasks.
Consider piloting or evaluating pharmacy-based counseling and faster-service models, since caregivers in this survey rated these above organisational conveniences such as apps or home delivery.

Because this is a single cross-sectional, non-representative sample with no severity or subgroup breakdown, treat these percentages as hypothesis-generating for local workflow review rather than as a validated benchmark.
policy: This evidence could inform discussion of whether existing community-nurse support programs should be scoped or funded to explicitly include communication and decision-support tasks in dementia medication management, not only physical/logistical caregiving.

Because no cost, utilization, or productivity data accompany these burden findings, any policy or funding discussion drawing on this study should be paired with separate cost or health-system utilization data before resource-allocation decisions are made.

Given the lack of subgroup breakdown (by caregiver sex, age, or relationship to patient) in this study, consider commissioning or drawing on disaggregated population survey data (such as that collected through NHIS or BRFSS in other contexts) if subgroup-specific caregiver burden patterns are relevant to a given policy question.

Treat the findings as specific to a self-selected German sample recruited through dementia caregiver self-help groups; generalizing to broader or different-country caregiver populations would be an extrapolation beyond what this survey supports.

inputs.label: Caregivers rating 'explaining medication info to patient' as (very) high burden
inputs.source: Document, Results section 'Components of the MP and their contribution to burden'; 0-100% range is an assumed exploration bound covering the full possible share, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's own reported share of caregivers who found explaining medication information to the patient very/highly burdensome, the single highest-rated task in the survey; moving it shows how sensitive the patient-facing burden average below is to this specific task.

inputs.label: Caregivers rating 'accompanying patient to appointments' as (very) high burden
inputs.source: Document, Results section 'Components of the MP and their contribution to burden'; 0-100% range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported share finding appointment accompaniment burdensome; it is one of three patient-facing tasks contributing to the patient-facing burden average below.

inputs.label: Caregivers rating 'reminding patient to take medication' as (very) high burden
inputs.source: Document, Results section 'Components of the MP and their contribution to burden'; 0-100% range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported share finding medication reminders burdensome; adjusting it tests how much this specific reminder task drives the overall patient-facing burden average below.

inputs.label: Caregivers rating 'obtaining medications from pharmacy' as (very) high burden
inputs.source: Document, Results section 'Components of the MP and their contribution to burden'; 0-100% range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported share finding the logistical task of obtaining medications burdensome, much lower than the patient-facing tasks; it anchors the logistical burden average below.

inputs.label: Caregivers rating 'organising/preparing medication doses' as (very) high burden
inputs.source: Document, Results section 'Components of the MP and their contribution to burden'; 0-100% range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported share finding dose preparation burdensome; it is the second component of the logistical burden average below.

inputs.label: General caregiver burden score (Zarit Burden Interview, short form)
inputs.source: Document, Table 1 (mean 14.6, SD 5.1); the 0-48 range is an assumed exploration bound reflecting a commonly scored range for this instrument type, not a range stated in this document.
inputs.interpretation: This is the validated general caregiver burden score the document reports for this sample; higher values mean greater overall self-reported caregiving strain, separate from the medication-specific tasks below, and the document found no statistically significant correlation between this score and medication-process burden.

inputs.label: Caregivers receiving community-nurse support with medication process
inputs.source: Document, Results section 'Influence of community nurses on burden'; 0-100% range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported share of caregivers who had community-nurse help with medication tasks; the document found no statistically significant difference in burden scores between caregivers with vs. without this support, so this input mainly illustrates current service reach rather than a proven burden-reducing lever.

inputs.label: Caregivers rating fast pharmacy service as (very) important
inputs.source: Document, Results section 'Informal caregivers' ratings of the importance of community pharmacy services'; 0-100% range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported share valuing fast pharmacy service; it is shown alongside the burden figures to illustrate which pharmacy service features caregivers prioritized most, for comparison against organisational services like delivery or app ordering discussed in the documentation.

outputs.label: Average share rating patient-facing medication tasks as (very) high burden
outputs.interpretation: This averages the document's three patient-facing task burden percentages (explaining medication info, accompanying to appointments, reminding about doses). A higher value means more of these communication- and decision-related tasks were widely felt as burdensome in this sample; the document reports all three individually in the 18-27% range.

outputs.label: Average share rating logistical medication tasks as (very) high burden
outputs.interpretation: This averages the document's two logistical task burden percentages (obtaining medications from the pharmacy, organising/preparing doses). A higher value would mean more caregivers found these practical tasks burdensome; the document reports both in the 4-6% range, notably lower than the patient-facing tasks.

outputs.label: Patient-facing minus logistical burden average (percentage points; positive = patient-facing tasks rated more burdensome, negative = logistical tasks rated more burdensome)
outputs.interpretation: This is the gap between the two averages above. In the document's own reported figures this gap is positive and substantial, reflecting that communication- and decision-related medication tasks were rated as burdensome by a much larger share of caregivers than purely logistical tasks; moving the sliders changes this gap illustratively but does not itself re-measure the underlying survey finding.

outputs.label: General caregiver burden (Zarit Burden Interview, short form)
outputs.interpretation: This passes through the document's validated general caregiver burden score (a composite scale, not specific to medication tasks). The document found no statistically significant correlation between this score and the medication-process burden percentages above (r=0.157, p=0.053, narrowly missing the study's own p<=0.05 threshold), so the two should be read as related but distinct findings, not combined into one metric.

outputs.label: Current community-nurse support coverage
outputs.interpretation: This passes through the document's reported share of caregivers currently receiving community-nurse help with medications. The document reports no statistically significant difference in either general burden (p=0.066, described by the authors as narrowly missing significance) or medication-process burden (p=0.595) between caregivers with vs. without this support, so a higher coverage value here does not, on the document's own evidence, imply lower burden.

scenarios.label: Universal nurse support
scenarios.goal: Tests whether raising community-nurse coverage to everyone would track with lower caregiver burden.
scenarios.description: If community-nurse support reached 100% of caregivers instead of the observed 37.8% (an illustrative upper bound, not a reported figure), coverage would rise accordingly, but the study's own non-significant comparisons (MP-related burden U=2896.0, p=0.595; general burden U=3837.5, p=0.066) mean burden outputs would not be expected to differ from the current mixed-coverage sample.

scenarios.label: No nurse support
scenarios.goal: Tests the opposite extreme of zero nurse coverage to illustrate the comparison group behind the study's null finding.
scenarios.description: If no caregivers received community-nurse support (0% coverage, an illustrative lower bound, not a reported figure) instead of the observed 37.8%, the study's own non-significant comparisons mean burden outputs would not be expected to differ from the current mixed-coverage sample either.

package.documentation:
## Data source
All figures come from a German nationwide cross-sectional survey of 180 informal caregivers of people with dementia, recruited through dementia caregiver self-help groups, examining burden from managing medications ('medication process' burden) and general caregiver burden (Zarit Burden Interview, short form). No dollar costs, caregiving hours, or income-loss figures were collected or are modeled here; every input and output is a self-reported percentage or scale score from this single survey.

## Inputs
Five inputs are the document's own reported percentages of caregivers rating specific medication-process tasks as very/highly burdensome: three patient-facing tasks (explaining medication information, accompanying to appointments, reminding about doses) and two logistical tasks (obtaining medications, organising/preparing doses). One input is the mean Zarit Burden Interview score (a validated general caregiver-strain scale; its own numeric range is not stated in the document, so the 0-48 slider bound used here is an assumed exploration range). One input is the share of caregivers currently receiving community-nurse support with medications. One input is the share rating fast pharmacy service as important, included for comparison with the burden figures and with other pharmacy-service preferences discussed in the document (thorough prescription counselling, 70.6%; OTC counselling, 62.6%; app/mail/phone ordering or delivery, about 40%) but not built as separate sliders here to keep the input count manageable.

## Outputs
Two averages (patient-facing vs. logistical task burden) and their difference reconstruct the document's central contrast. A pass-through of the Zarit score and of nurse-support coverage are included for reference; the document reports neither correlates significantly with medication-process burden.

## Limitations
This is a single cross-sectional, non-representative convenience sample with no long-term follow-up; findings should not be generalized beyond German caregivers connected to self-help groups. The pooled percentages and mean Zarit score reported here have not been checked by the document for variation by caregiver sex, age, or relationship to the patient; federal survey data such as NHIS and BRFSS generally supports this kind of disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform one. Separately, the document notes that current community-nurse support addresses physical/logistical caregiving but, by the authors' own account, 'may not directly address the interpersonal and decision-related components that drive' medication-process burden - a gap in how existing support services are structured, distinct from any accuracy or funding issue with the burden estimates themselves.

spec.title: Dementia Caregiver Medication-Process Burden (German Survey, n=180)
spec.boundary: This simulation reflects a German nationwide cross-sectional survey of 180 informal caregivers of people with dementia, examining self-reported burden from medication-related tasks ('medication process' burden) and a validated general caregiver burden score (Zarit Burden Interview, short form). It covers only self-reported percentages and scale scores from this single survey wave; it does not include any dollar costs, caregiving hours, income loss, or federal/national data, and findings should not be generalized beyond caregivers recruited through German dementia self-help groups.

takeaway.patient: In this survey of 180 family caregivers of people with dementia in Germany, caregivers rated tasks that involve talking with the patient about medicines, going along to doctor visits, and reminding about doses as more tiring than simply picking up prescriptions or organizing pill doses. Caregivers who already had help from a community nurse did not report meaningfully less burden overall or with medication tasks specifically than those without that help, so nurse support alone may not address these communication-heavy parts of care. Caregivers also said fast service and thorough counseling from the pharmacy mattered more to them than delivery or app-based ordering.
takeaway.care: Among surveyed informal caregivers (n=180), interpersonal and decision-related medication tasks - explaining medication information, accompanying to appointments, and reminding about doses - were rated as burdensome by a much larger share of caregivers (18-27%) than purely logistical tasks such as collecting prescriptions or preparing doses (4-6%). Current community-nurse support, received by about 38% of caregivers, was not associated with a statistically significant reduction in either general caregiver burden or medication-process burden, suggesting existing nursing support may be addressing physical/logistical care needs without touching the communication and decision-support components driving burden. Caregivers also prioritized fast service and in-depth counseling from community pharmacies well above organisational conveniences like apps or delivery.
takeaway.policy: This survey-based evidence indicates that within this German sample, medication-related caregiver burden is concentrated in communication and decision-support tasks rather than logistics, and that current community-nurse support coverage (about 38% of caregivers) is not statistically associated with lower general or medication-process burden scores. No cost, utilization, or productivity data were collected, so this cannot support cost-effectiveness or budget-impact conclusions; it instead points to a gap in how existing community-based support services are structured relative to where caregivers report the most strain.

patient: If you support someone with dementia's medications, consider raising with your care team which specific tasks feel hardest for you - explaining medicine information, going to appointments, or reminders - rather than assuming all medication help needs are the same.

If a community nurse is already involved, this survey's finding suggests their support may not by itself reduce the communication-heavy parts of medication management; it may be worth asking what additional support exists for those specific tasks.

When choosing or evaluating a pharmacy, you may want to ask about wait times and the depth of medication counseling offered, since caregivers in this survey valued those over delivery or app-based ordering.
Keep in mind this reflects one German survey of caregivers connected to self-help groups; your own experience and what is available to you may differ.
care: This finding on which medication-process tasks caregivers rate as most burdensome (communication and appointment-related tasks vs. logistics) may be worth checking against your own program's service mix before assuming logistical support (delivery, prescription pickup) is what caregivers need most.

Given that community-nurse involvement was not associated with lower burden on these specific tasks in this sample, consider whether nurse training or care-coordination protocols could be extended to cover communication and decision-support roles, rather than only physical/logistical caregiving tasks.
Consider piloting or evaluating pharmacy-based counseling and faster-service models, since caregivers in this survey rated these above organisational conveniences such as apps or home delivery.

Because this is a single cross-sectional, non-representative sample with no severity or subgroup breakdown, treat these percentages as hypothesis-generating for local workflow review rather than as a validated benchmark.
policy: This evidence could inform discussion of whether existing community-nurse support programs should be scoped or funded to explicitly include communication and decision-support tasks in dementia medication management, not only physical/logistical caregiving.

Because no cost, utilization, or productivity data accompany these burden findings, any policy or funding discussion drawing on this study should be paired with separate cost or health-system utilization data before resource-allocation decisions are made.

Given the lack of subgroup breakdown (by caregiver sex, age, or relationship to patient) in this study, consider commissioning or drawing on disaggregated population survey data (such as that collected through NHIS or BRFSS in other contexts) if subgroup-specific caregiver burden patterns are relevant to a given policy question.

Treat the findings as specific to a self-selected German sample recruited through dementia caregiver self-help groups; generalizing to broader or different-country caregiver populations would be an extrapolation beyond what this survey supports.

inputs.label: Caregivers rating 'explaining medication info to patient' as (very) high burden
inputs.source: Document, Results section 'Components of the MP and their contribution to burden'; 0-100% range is an assumed exploration bound covering the full possible share, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's own reported share of caregivers who found explaining medication information to the patient very/highly burdensome, the single highest-rated task in the survey; moving it shows how sensitive the patient-facing burden average below is to this specific task.

inputs.label: Caregivers rating 'accompanying patient to appointments' as (very) high burden
inputs.source: Document, Results section 'Components of the MP and their contribution to burden'; 0-100% range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported share finding appointment accompaniment burdensome; it is one of three patient-facing tasks contributing to the patient-facing burden average below.

inputs.label: Caregivers rating 'reminding patient to take medication' as (very) high burden
inputs.source: Document, Results section 'Components of the MP and their contribution to burden'; 0-100% range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported share finding medication reminders burdensome; adjusting it tests how much this specific reminder task drives the overall patient-facing burden average below.

inputs.label: Caregivers rating 'obtaining medications from pharmacy' as (very) high burden
inputs.source: Document, Results section 'Components of the MP and their contribution to burden'; 0-100% range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported share finding the logistical task of obtaining medications burdensome, much lower than the patient-facing tasks; it anchors the logistical burden average below.

inputs.label: Caregivers rating 'organising/preparing medication doses' as (very) high burden
inputs.source: Document, Results section 'Components of the MP and their contribution to burden'; 0-100% range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported share finding dose preparation burdensome; it is the second component of the logistical burden average below.

inputs.label: General caregiver burden score (Zarit Burden Interview, short form)
inputs.source: Document, Table 1 (mean 14.6, SD 5.1); the 0-48 range is an assumed exploration bound reflecting a commonly scored range for this instrument type, not a range stated in this document.
inputs.interpretation: This is the validated general caregiver burden score the document reports for this sample; higher values mean greater overall self-reported caregiving strain, separate from the medication-specific tasks below, and the document found no statistically significant correlation between this score and medication-process burden.

inputs.label: Caregivers receiving community-nurse support with medication process
inputs.source: Document, Results section 'Influence of community nurses on burden'; 0-100% range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported share of caregivers who had community-nurse help with medication tasks; the document found no statistically significant difference in burden scores between caregivers with vs. without this support, so this input mainly illustrates current service reach rather than a proven burden-reducing lever.

inputs.label: Caregivers rating fast pharmacy service as (very) important
inputs.source: Document, Results section 'Informal caregivers' ratings of the importance of community pharmacy services'; 0-100% range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported share valuing fast pharmacy service; it is shown alongside the burden figures to illustrate which pharmacy service features caregivers prioritized most, for comparison against organisational services like delivery or app ordering discussed in the documentation.

outputs.label: Average share rating patient-facing medication tasks as (very) high burden
outputs.interpretation: This averages the document's three patient-facing task burden percentages (explaining medication info, accompanying to appointments, reminding about doses). A higher value means more of these communication- and decision-related tasks were widely felt as burdensome in this sample; the document reports all three individually in the 18-27% range.

outputs.label: Average share rating logistical medication tasks as (very) high burden
outputs.interpretation: This averages the document's two logistical task burden percentages (obtaining medications from the pharmacy, organising/preparing doses). A higher value would mean more caregivers found these practical tasks burdensome; the document reports both in the 4-6% range, notably lower than the patient-facing tasks.

outputs.label: Patient-facing minus logistical burden average (percentage points; positive = patient-facing tasks rated more burdensome, negative = logistical tasks rated more burdensome)
outputs.interpretation: This is the gap between the two averages above. In the document's own reported figures this gap is positive and substantial, reflecting that communication- and decision-related medication tasks were rated as burdensome by a much larger share of caregivers than purely logistical tasks; moving the sliders changes this gap illustratively but does not itself re-measure the underlying survey finding.

outputs.label: General caregiver burden (Zarit Burden Interview, short form)
outputs.interpretation: This passes through the document's validated general caregiver burden score (a composite scale, not specific to medication tasks). The document found no statistically significant correlation between this score and the medication-process burden percentages above (r=0.157, p=0.053, narrowly missing the study's own p<=0.05 threshold), so the two should be read as related but distinct findings, not combined into one metric.

outputs.label: Current community-nurse support coverage
outputs.interpretation: This passes through the document's reported share of caregivers currently receiving community-nurse help with medications. The document reports no statistically significant difference in either general burden (p=0.066, described by the authors as narrowly missing significance) or medication-process burden (p=0.595) between caregivers with vs. without this support, so a higher coverage value here does not, on the document's own evidence, imply lower burden.

scenarios.label: Universal nurse support
scenarios.goal: Tests whether raising community-nurse coverage to everyone would track with lower caregiver burden.
scenarios.description: If community-nurse support reached 100% of caregivers instead of the observed 37.8% (an illustrative upper bound, not a reported figure), coverage would rise accordingly, but the study's own non-significant comparisons (MP-related burden U=2896.0, p=0.595; general burden U=3837.5, p=0.066) mean burden outputs would not be expected to differ from the current mixed-coverage sample.

scenarios.label: No nurse support
scenarios.goal: Tests the opposite extreme of zero nurse coverage to illustrate the comparison group behind the study's null finding.
scenarios.description: If no caregivers received community-nurse support (0% coverage, an illustrative lower bound, not a reported figure) instead of the observed 37.8%, the study's own non-significant comparisons mean burden outputs would not be expected to differ from the current mixed-coverage sample either.
